docs.title: vexy-python-markdown-steroids
docs.text:
vexy-python-markdown-steroids is a set of twelve extensions for Python-Markdown. You install the package from PyPI as vexy-python-markdown-steroids, and import the extensions from the mdx_steroids package.

Each extension is a separate module. You turn it on by adding its dotted name, such as mdx_steroids.keys, to the list of extensions in Python, in the python -m markdown command, or in the markdown_extensions list of an MkDocs site.

docs.title: One extension, from input to output
docs.text:
The keys extension turns key combinations into <kbd> elements. This Markdown:

Press ++ctrl+s++.

becomes this HTML with extensions=["mdx_steroids.keys"]:

<p>Press <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-control">Ctrl</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-s">S</kbd></span>.</p>

The extension recognised ctrl as an alias of the key control, printed it as Ctrl, and gave each key a CSS class you can style.

docs.title: The extensions
docs.text:
Extension What it does Stage absimgsrc Prepends a base URL to relative image paths Tree processor comments Removes <!--- … --> comments, keeps <!-- … --> Preprocessor figcap Turns titled images into <figure> with <figcaption> Inline pattern, tree processor img_smart Reads image sizes, sets width and classes, adds lightbox links Block processor interlink Adds a prefix and suffix to short internal link targets Preprocessor keys (alias kbd) Renders ++ctrl+s++ as <kbd> elements Inline pattern kill_tags Deletes HTML elements by CSS or XPath selector, and empty elements Postprocessor md_mako Runs the Markdown through the Mako template engine Preprocessor meta_yaml Reads a YAML front-matter block into md.Meta Preprocessor replimgsrc Find-and-replace in image src attributes Tree processor translate_no Adds translate="no" to code, keys and other elements Postprocessor wikilink Turns [[Page Name]] into a Markdown link Preprocessor

The "Stage" column says where in the Python-Markdown pipeline the extension works. Architecture explains the stages and the order in which the extensions run.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Every module in mdx_steroids is an independent Python-Markdown extension. This page explains where each one hooks into Python-Markdown's conversion and in which order they run when you load several.

docs.title: The Python-Markdown pipeline
docs.text:
Python-Markdown converts text in five stages. Each stage has a registry of processors, and processors with a higher priority run first.

Stage Works on Runs Preprocessors The source, as a list of lines First Block processors Blocks of lines, building an element tree Second Inline patterns Text inside the elements Third Tree processors The finished element tree Fourth Postprocessors The serialised HTML string Last

docs.title: Where each extension runs
docs.text:
Extension Stage Registered name Priority meta_yaml Preprocessor meta_yaml 29 md_mako Preprocessor md_mako 28 comments Preprocessor comment_munger 25 comments Preprocessor comment_remover 15 interlink Preprocessor interlink 6 wikilink Preprocessor wikilink 4 img_smart Block processor smartImage 75 keys Inline pattern keys 185 figcap Inline pattern image_link (replaces the built-in pattern) 150 figcap Tree processor definition_caption 6 absimgsrc Tree processor absoluteImages 0 replimgsrc Tree processor ReplaceImageSrc 0 comments Postprocessor raw_comment_replacer 5 kill_tags Postprocessor kill_tags 0 translate_no Postprocessor translate_no 0

Processors with the same priority run in the order their extensions were loaded.

docs.title: What the order means in practice
docs.text:
• Front matter, then templates. meta_yaml (29) runs before md_mako (28), so the YAML block is gone and md.Meta is filled when Mako renders the page.
  • Templates, then links. md_mako runs before interlink and wikilink, so a template can produce [[Page]] links and they are still converted.
  • Comments after templates. comments removes <!--- … --> after Mako has run. A Mako expression inside a three-dash comment is still evaluated, and an undefined variable there still stops the conversion.
  • Line-based preprocessors see code. comments, interlink, wikilink and md_mako work on raw lines, before Python-Markdown knows what is code. Their syntax is also processed inside indented code blocks and inline code. See each extension's page for details.
  • Images. img_smart (block processor) builds its own <img> for images that stand alone on a line. figcap changes images in running text. Both produce <img> elements that absimgsrc and replimgsrc change later.
  • HTML clean-up last. kill_tags and translate_no work on the final HTML string, so they also see raw HTML from the source and elements created by other extensions, such as the <kbd> elements from keys.

docs.title: Module layout
docs.text:
File Contents mdx_steroids/__init__.py __version__ (from __version__.py, generated by hatch-vcs) and __all__ mdx_steroids/<name>.py One extension per module, with a makeExtension() function mdx_steroids/kbd.py from .keys import *, which makes mdx_steroids.kbd an alias of keys mdx_steroids/keymap_db.py keymap (key name → displayed text) and aliases (alias → key name) mdx_steroids/util.py Re-exports pymdownx.util

Python-Markdown loads an extension by its dotted name: it imports the module and calls its makeExtension(**options).

docs.title: How the options reach the processors
docs.text: Each extension class defines its options in self.config as {"name": [default, "description"]}. Python-Markdown's Extension class merges the values you pass. Most extensions then hand self.getConfigs(), a plain {"name": value} dict, to their processor. interlink and wikilink hand over self.config itself and read values with config[name][0].

docs.title: Set up a development environment
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository. The default branch is master.

    git clone https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-python-markdown-steroids.git
cd vexy-python-markdown-steroids

  2. Create the environment with the package and its development tools (pytest, pytest-cov, ruff):

    uv sync --extra dev

docs.title: Run the tests
docs.text:
uv run python -m pytest -q

There is one test file per extension in tests/, for example tests/test_keys.py and tests/test_md_mako.py, plus tests/test_version.py and tests/test_issue102_rendering.py. The suite has 163 tests.

With coverage:

uv run python -m pytest --cov=mdx_steroids --cov-report=term-missing

docs.title: Add or change an extension
docs.text:
1. Put the extension in its own module, mdx_steroids/<name>.py.
  2. Define options in the extension class as self.config = {"option": [default, "description"]} and call super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) afterwards.
  3. Register processors in extendMarkdown(self, md) with an explicit priority. Check the priority table so the new processor runs at the right moment relative to the others.
  4. Add a module-level makeExtension(*args, **kwargs) that returns the extension.
  5. Add tests/test_<name>.py with input Markdown and the expected HTML.
  6. Add a page in src_docs/md/extensions/ and list it in the nav of src_docs/mkdocs.yml.

New source files start with a this_file: comment that gives their path.

docs.title: Build the package and the documentation
docs.text:
./build.sh            # documentation and package
./build.sh docs       # documentation only, into docs/
./build.sh package    # dist/*.whl and dist/*.tar.gz, then twine check

The documentation source is in src_docs/md/, its configuration in src_docs/mkdocs.yml. src_docs/build.sh builds it with ProperDocs and the MaterialX theme in strict mode, so a broken link or any other warning fails the build. For a live preview that also reloads when files in mdx_steroids/ change:

Do not edit docs/ by hand. The Docs workflow rebuilds it and commits it after every push to master that changes src_docs/. GitHub Pages serves it at https://vexy.dev/vexy-python-markdown-steroids/.

The version comes from the latest vX.Y.Z git tag through hatch-vcs. ./publish.sh makes a release:

  1. uvx gitnextver commits pending changes, tags the next vX.Y.Z and pushes.
  2. ./build.sh package builds the wheel and source distribution.
  3. uv publish dist/* uploads them to PyPI. It needs UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN or another uv publish credential.

docs.title: absimgsrc
docs.text: mdx_steroids.absimgsrc prepends a base URL to every relative image path. Use it when the images of a document are served from another host, such as a CDN, or when the same HTML is shown at several URL depths.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With base_url: https://cdn.example.com/docs, this Markdown:

![Alt text](images/photo.jpg)

![x](/abs/a.png)

![y](https://ex.com/b.png)

becomes:

<p><img alt="Alt text" src="https://cdn.example.com/docs/images/photo.jpg" /></p>
<p><img alt="x" src="https://cdn.example.com/abs/a.png" /></p>
<p><img alt="y" src="https://ex.com/b.png" /></p>

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
After Python-Markdown has built the document tree, the extension visits every <img> element that has a src attribute.

  1. It checks whether the src is relative. A src is absolute, and left alone, if it starts with http or //, or with one of these schemes: ftp://, ftps://, mailto:, news:, telnet://, file://, data:, tel:, ssh://, sftp://.
  2. If base_url is empty, it leaves the src alone.
  3. If base_url does not end with / and the path does not start with /, it adds a / to base_url.
  4. It joins the two with Python's urllib.parse.urljoin() and writes the result back to src.

Because of step 4, a path that starts with / replaces the whole path of base_url: /abs/a.png with base https://cdn.example.com/docs gives https://cdn.example.com/abs/a.png, as in the example above.

The extension only changes images written in Markdown syntax. An <img> tag written as raw HTML in the Markdown source, such as <img src="raw.png">, keeps its src, because raw HTML is not part of the document tree.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning base_url str "" The URL to put in front of relative image paths. Empty means "change nothing".

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    "![Alt text](images/photo.jpg)",
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.absimgsrc"],
    extension_configs={"mdx_steroids.absimgsrc": {"base_url": "https://cdn.example.com/"}},
)
# <p><img alt="Alt text" src="https://cdn.example.com/images/photo.jpg" /></p>

MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.absimgsrc:
      base_url: https://cdn.example.com/

Warning

In MkDocs, absolute image URLs are not checked or copied by MkDocs. Make sure the images exist at the new location.

docs.title: comments
docs.text:
mdx_steroids.comments removes comments that start with three dashes, <!---, from the output. Ordinary HTML comments, <!--, stay in the HTML. Use the three-dash form for notes to yourself and other writers.

The extension has no options.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
This Markdown:

Visible.

<!--- removed -->

<!-- kept -->

Text <!--- inline gone --> end.

<!---
multi
line
-->
After.

becomes:

<p>Visible.</p>
<!-- kept -->

<p>Text end.</p>
<p>After.</p>
  • The block comment <!--- removed --> is gone.
  • The ordinary comment <!-- kept --> is still in the HTML.
  • The inline comment and the whitespace before it are gone; Text end. remains.
  • The comment that spans three lines is gone, and the text after --> stays.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension works on the source text, in three steps:

  1. Protect. A preprocessor replaces every <!--- with a placeholder string, so that Python-Markdown does not treat it as an HTML comment.
  2. Remove. A second preprocessor removes everything from a placeholder up to the next -->, together with the whitespace before the placeholder. If there is no --> on the same line, it removes the rest of the line and every following line up to the line that contains -->. Text after that --> is kept.
  3. Restore. A postprocessor turns any placeholder that is left in the HTML back into <!---.

docs.title: Comments inside code
docs.text:
Step 2 runs on the raw source, so it can also reach code. With extensions=["mdx_steroids.comments", "fenced_code"]:

Source Result A fenced code block (```) that contains <!--- x --> Kept. fenced_code stores the block before step 2 runs, and step 3 restores <!---. An indented code block that contains <!--- x --> The comment is removed from the code. Inline code such as `<!---` with no --> on the line Starts a multi-line comment. Everything up to the next -->, even in later paragraphs, is removed.

To show the three-dash marker in running text, put it in a fenced code block or write it as <!---.

  - mdx_steroids.comments

docs.title: figcap
docs.text:
mdx_steroids.figcap turns an image that has a title into an HTML5 <figure> with the title as its <figcaption>. It also turns an image followed by a definition-list caption into a figure.

The extension has no options.

docs.title: Caption from the image title
docs.text:
The title is the quoted text after the image path. This Markdown:

![A cat](cat.jpg "Our office cat")

![No title](dog.jpg)

becomes:

<p>
<figure><img alt="A cat" src="cat.jpg" title="Our office cat" /><figcaption>Our office cat</figcaption>
</figure>
</p>
<p><img alt="No title" src="dog.jpg" /></p>
  • The image with a title is wrapped in <figure>, and the title is repeated in <figcaption>. The title attribute stays on the <img>.
  • The image without a title is left as it is.

Note

The figure stays inside the paragraph that Python-Markdown creates for the image, so the output has <figure> inside <p>. Browsers display this, but it is not valid HTML. Use the definition-list form below if you need a figure outside a paragraph.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension registers its own inline pattern under the name image_link, which replaces Python-Markdown's standard pattern for ![alt](src "title"). It lets the standard code build the <img>, then checks for a title. If there is one, it returns a <figure> with the image and a <figcaption> instead of the bare image.

Reference-style images (![alt][ref]) use another pattern and are not changed.

docs.title: Caption from a definition list
docs.text:
With Python-Markdown's def_list extension also loaded, write the caption as a definition of the image:

![A cat](cat.jpg)
:   Our office cat

This becomes a figure without a surrounding paragraph:

<figure>
<img alt="A cat" src="cat.jpg" /><figcaption>Our office cat</figcaption>
</figure>

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
After the document tree is built, a tree processor looks at every <dl> element. It converts the list when every term (<dt>) contains only images and no text, and every term is followed by exactly one definition (<dd>):

  • A list with one image and one caption becomes one <figure>.
  • A list with several image–caption pairs becomes a <div> with one <figure> per pair.
  • Each <dd> becomes the <figcaption>, so the caption can contain inline formatting.

Any other definition list is left unchanged.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(text, extensions=["mdx_steroids.figcap", "def_list"])

MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - def_list
  - mdx_steroids.figcap

docs.title: img_smart
docs.text: mdx_steroids.img_smart replaces an image that stands alone in a paragraph with an <img> whose width and CSS classes are based on the real size of the image file. Large images are wrapped in a link for a lightbox script. The extension can also rewrite the image path, add loading="lazy", turn the alt text into a caption and cache image sizes in a JSON file.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Take a PNG image, img/wide.png, that is 1200 × 300 pixels, and these options:

lazy: true
alt_figure: true
cache: cache.json

This Markdown:

![Wide image](img/wide.png)

becomes:

<figure><a class="fancybox" data-caption="Wide image" data-fancybox="help" href="img/wide.png"><img alt="Wide image" class="image iml" loading="lazy" src="img/wide.png" width="600" /></a><figcaption>Wide image</figcaption>
</figure>

While it works, the extension prints Analyzing image: img/wide.png with size 1127 to standard output, and it writes this to cache.json:

{"img/wide.png": {"media": "img", "width": 1200, "height": 300}}

What happened:

  1. The extension read the file and found a width of 1200 pixels.
  2. It divided the width by the default scale of 2 and set width="600".
  3. 600 is more than 500, so it added the class iml and wrapped the image in a lightbox link.
  4. lazy: true added loading="lazy".
  5. alt_figure: true wrapped everything in a <figure> with the alt text as caption.

docs.title: Which images it handles
docs.text:
The extension is a block processor. It handles a block only when the whole block is one line that contains nothing but an image, optionally followed by an attribute list:

![Alt text](path/to/image.png)
![Alt text](path/to/image.png){: width=400 .shadow }

Images inside running text, and blocks with more than one line, are left to Python-Markdown. The resulting element is added directly to the document, not inside a <p>.

docs.title: Reading the size
docs.text:
The extension looks up the size in this order:

  1. In the cache, if cache names a JSON file and the file has an entry for the image path.
  2. From the file itself. A path that starts with http is downloaded with requests. Any other path is opened as a local file, relative to the current working directory. If the file does not exist, the size is unknown.

Then it decides what the file is:

  • If it contains <svg and </svg>, it is an SVG. The size comes from the viewBox attribute.
  • If it contains <html and </html>, it prints WARNING: <path> is of type HTML, possibly 404 and the size is unknown.
  • Otherwise filetype guesses the type. Images are measured with imageio; videos are measured with imageio's pyav plugin, which needs the separate av package.

If the size is larger than 1920 × 1080, it is scaled down proportionally to fit 1920 × 1080.

docs.title: Scale
docs.text:
The displayed width is the image width divided by a scale. The default scale is 2, which suits images saved at double resolution. The scale changes when the attribute list contains:

Attribute Effect width=N The width becomes N and the scale becomes 1 height=N The height becomes N .lores (class) The scale becomes 1 data-scale=N% The scale becomes 100 / N; data-scale=25% gives 4, so a 1200-pixel image gets width="300"

data-scale is not copied to the HTML. All other attributes and classes in the list are copied to the <img>; a width you set is then replaced by the computed width.

docs.title: Width and classes
docs.text:
Every image gets the class image. The extension then compares the displayed width (width / scale):

Displayed width width attribute Extra class Lightbox link More than 1280 displayed width imxl yes 501 to 1280 displayed width iml yes 33 to 500 displayed width imm no 1 to 32 (image width not 0) image width ims no Size unknown none none no

The lightbox link is <a class="fancybox" data-fancybox="help" href="…"> with a data-caption taken from the image title, or from the alt text if there is no title. It works with the Fancybox script, which you add to the page yourself.

The image title (![alt](src "title")) is not written to the <img>. It is only used for data-caption.

docs.title: Examples of sizes
docs.text: Markdown File size Result ![Small image](img/small.png) 200 × 100 <img alt="Small image" class="image imm" src="img/small.png" width="100" /> ![Sized](img/wide.png){: width=400 .shadow } 1200 × 300 <img alt="Sized" class="shadow image imm" src="img/wide.png" width="400" /> ![Missing](nope.png) file not found <img alt="Missing" class="image" src="nope.png" />

docs.title: Rewriting the path
docs.text:
find, repl_path and repl_url let the path in the Markdown differ from both the file on disk and the URL in the HTML:

  • find is the text to look for in the image path.
  • repl_path replaces find to get the local file path to measure.
  • repl_url replaces find to get the src written to the HTML.

With find: /media/, repl_path: img/ and repl_url: https://cdn.example.com/img/:

![Shot](/media/small.png)

The extension measures img/small.png and writes:

<img alt="Shot" class="image imm" src="https://cdn.example.com/img/small.png" width="100" />

The cache uses the local file path (after repl_path) as its key.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning find str "" Text to replace in the image path. Nothing is replaced when empty. repl_path str "" Replacement for find when building the local file path. repl_url str "" Replacement for find when building the src URL. alt_figure bool false Wrap the result in <figure> with the alt text as <figcaption>. cache str "" Path of a JSON file that stores image sizes between runs. The file is read and rewritten for every handled image. lazy bool false Add loading="lazy" to the <img>.

docs.title: Configuration example
docs.text:
MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - attr_list
  - mdx_steroids.img_smart:
      find: /media/
      repl_path: src_docs/md/media/
      repl_url: /media/
      cache: .img_cache.json
      lazy: true

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The extension prints progress messages with print(), not through logging.
  • Only images whose size is known are written to the cache.
  • A failed download is ignored silently; the image then has no size.

docs.title: interlink
docs.text: mdx_steroids.interlink lets you write short internal links, such as [Setup](setup), and turns them into full URLs by adding a prefix and a suffix. Links that contain a protocol or a period are left alone.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With base_url: /docs/ and end_url: /, this Markdown:

See [setup](setup#install), [home](index), [ext](https://ex.com), [file](a.html).

becomes:

<p>See <a href="/docs/setup/#install">setup</a>, <a href="/docs/index/">home</a>, <a href="https://ex.com">ext</a>, <a href="a.html">file</a>.</p>
  • setup#install became /docs/setup/#install: the suffix goes before the anchor.
  • https://ex.com contains :// and was not changed.
  • a.html contains a period and was not changed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension is a preprocessor: it rewrites the Markdown source before Python-Markdown parses it. On every line, it looks for inline links of the form [text](target), where target contains no spaces. Image links (![…](…)) are skipped.

For each link:

  1. If the target contains :// or ., the link is left as it is.
  2. The target is split at #. If the part before # is empty (a link to an anchor on the same page, such as #intro), the link is left as it is.
  3. Otherwise the new target is base_url + page + end_url, followed by # and the anchor if there was one.

The rewritten link is ordinary Markdown, so Python-Markdown then turns it into an <a> element as usual.

Because the extension works on raw lines, it also rewrites links inside code blocks and inline code. Links with a title ([text](target "title")) contain a space and are not matched.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Meaning base_url str "" Text put before the page name. end_url str "" Text put after the page name, before any #anchor.

With both options empty, the extension changes nothing.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    "See [setup](setup#install).",
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.interlink"],
    extension_configs={"mdx_steroids.interlink": {"base_url": "/docs/", "end_url": "/"}},
)
# <p>See <a href="/docs/setup/#install">setup</a>.</p>

MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.interlink:
      base_url: /docs/
      end_url: /

This page lists every key name that keys knows, taken from mdx_steroids/keymap_db.py ("English US keymap, revised 2019-11-18 by Adam Twardoch"). Write a name between ++ and ++, for example ++page-up++.

  • Key name is what you type. It also becomes the CSS class key-<name>.
  • Displayed text is the text inside the <kbd> element.

Names are matched in lower case, so ++Ctrl++ and ++CTRL++ work. With camel_case: true, ++PageUp++ is read as ++page-up++. Use the key_map option to add names or change the displayed text.

Note

docs.title: keys
docs.text: mdx_steroids.keys renders keyboard input. Write keys between ++ and ++, joined with +, and the extension turns them into <kbd> elements with a CSS class per key. It is a fork of pymdownx.keys by Isaac Muse with its own key list (see Key name reference).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With camel_case: true, this Markdown:

Press ++Shift+Alt+PgUp++, type in ++"Hello"++ and press ++Enter++.

becomes:

<p>Press <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-shift">Shift</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-alt">Alt</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-page-up">PgUp</kbd></span>, type in <span class="keys"><kbd>Hello</kbd></span> and press <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-enter">Enter</kbd></span>.</p>
  • Each key became a <kbd> with the class key-<name> and the displayed text from the key list.
  • PgUp is an alias of page-up, so its class is key-page-up.
  • "Hello" is a quoted string, so it became a <kbd> with the text as written and no key- class.
  • The whole group is wrapped in <span class="keys">, and <span>+</span> separates the keys.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
Markdown Meaning ++enter++ One key ++ctrl+alt+del++ A combination; keys are joined with + ++"Hello world"++ or ++'Hello'++ Text to type, shown as written ++ctrl+"c"++ Keys and quoted text can be mixed \++ctrl++ A backslash before ++ keeps the text literal: ++ctrl++

Key names may contain letters, digits, _ and -. Inside quotes, a backslash escapes the next character.

docs.title: How a key is looked up
docs.text:
For each unquoted key name, the extension:

  1. Converts the name to lower case. With camel_case: true, it instead inserts a hyphen before each capital letter that follows another character and then lowers it, so PageUp becomes page-up and pageUp becomes page-up.
  2. Replaces an alias with its key name, for example ctrl with control.
  3. Looks the key name up in the key list, merged with your key_map.

If any key of a group is not found, the whole group is left as plain text. For example, ++ctrl+foo++ stays ++ctrl+foo++ in the output, and without camel_case, ++PageUp++ stays as it is, because pageup is not a key name.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning separator str "+" Text placed between keys, inside <span>. An empty string leaves the separator out. strict bool false false: wrap the group in <span>. true: wrap it in <kbd>, which follows the HTML5 rule for nested keyboard input. class str "keys" Class(es) of the outer element, separated by spaces. camel_case bool false Read PageUp as page-up. key_map dict {} Extra keys, or new displayed text for existing keys: {"name": "Displayed text"}.

docs.title: strict and separator
docs.text:
With strict: true and separator: "":

Press ++ctrl+s++.

<p>Press <kbd class="keys"><kbd class="key-control">Ctrl</kbd><kbd class="key-s">S</kbd></kbd>.</p>

With separator: " + " and class: "keys shortcut":

Press ++ctrl+alt+del++.

<p>Press <span class="keys shortcut"><kbd class="key-control">Ctrl</kbd><span> + </span><kbd class="key-alt">Alt</kbd><span> + </span><kbd class="key-delete">Del</kbd></span>.</p>

docs.title: key_map
docs.text:
With key_map: {hyper: Hyper}:

Press ++hyper+s++.

<p>Press <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-hyper">Hyper</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-s">S</kbd></span>.</p>

Aliases are applied before key_map is consulted. A key_map entry for an alias name, such as ctrl, has no effect; use the key name, control.

docs.title: The kbd alias
docs.text:
mdx_steroids.kbd re-exports everything from mdx_steroids.keys. Loading either name gives the same extension with the same options:

markdown.markdown("Press ++ctrl+s++.", extensions=["mdx_steroids.kbd"])

docs.title: Styling
docs.text:
The extension only produces markup. Style it with CSS, for example:

.keys kbd {
  border: 1px solid #d1d5da;
  border-radius: 3px;
  box-shadow: inset 0 -1px 0 #d1d5da;
  padding: 0.2em 0.4em;
  font-family: monospace;
}

Each key also has its own class, such as .key-control or .key-enter, if you want to show icons for some keys.

docs.title: Use with other extensions
docs.text:
• Do not load pymdownx.keys together with this extension. Both use the ++…++ syntax and register their inline pattern under the same name, keys, so only one of them takes effect.
  • translate_no marks <kbd> elements by default, so browser translation leaves key names alone.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.keys:
      camel_case: true
      separator: " + "

Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    "Press ++ctrl+s++.",
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.keys"],
    extension_configs={"mdx_steroids.keys": {"strict": True}},
)

docs.title: kill_tags
docs.text: mdx_steroids.kill_tags deletes HTML elements from the finished output. You choose the elements with CSS selectors or XPath expressions. It also deletes elements that are empty, such as a <p> with nothing in it.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With kill: [".ad"] and kill_known: true, this Markdown:

Keep this <del>but not this</del>.

<p></p>

<div class="ad">Advert</div>

End.

becomes (blank lines shortened):

<p>Keep this .</p>

<p>End.</p>
  • <del>but not this</del> was removed by the built-in selectors that kill_known: true adds. The text after it, ., was kept.
  • <div class="ad"> matched the selector .ad and was removed with its content.
  • The empty <p></p> was removed because p is in the default kill_empty list.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension is a postprocessor: it runs on the HTML string after Python-Markdown has serialised the document.

  1. If normalize is true, it reparses the HTML with BeautifulSoup and html5lib.
  2. It parses the HTML as a fragment with lxml, inside a temporary <div>.
  3. It converts each entry of kill to XPath. An entry that starts with ! is used as XPath directly; any other entry is a CSS selector and is converted with cssselect.
  4. With kill_known: true, it adds two built-in XPath expressions (see below).
  5. It removes every element that matches, with its content. Text that followed the element (its "tail") is kept and attached to the previous element or to the parent.
  6. For each tag name in kill_empty, it removes elements of that name that contain no text (other than whitespace) and have no attributes, at any depth.
  7. It serialises the fragment back to HTML. If normalize is true, it runs BeautifulSoup over the result again.

docs.title: The known selectors
docs.text:
kill_known: true adds these two XPath expressions:

//pre[@class and contains(concat(' ', normalize-space(@class), ' '), ' highlight ') and code[@class and contains(concat(' ', normalize-space(@class), ' '), ' language-del ')]]
descendant-or-self::del

The first removes a highlighted code block whose language is del. The second removes every <del> element. Together they let you keep text in the Markdown source, visible in a plain preview such as GitHub, that never reaches the built HTML:

Visible paragraph.

```del
This block is visible on GitHub but removed from the HTML.
```

Visible ~~on GitHub only~~ text.

The first expression only matches <pre class="highlight"><code class="language-del">. pymdownx.superfences produces that markup when pymdownx.highlight has use_pygments: false. With Pygments turned on (the default), the class highlight sits on a surrounding <div> and the block is not removed. The ~~text~~ form needs pymdownx.tilde, which turns it into <del>.

This configuration removes both parts of the example above:

markdown_extensions:
  - pymdownx.highlight:
      use_pygments: false
  - pymdownx.superfences
  - pymdownx.tilde
  - mdx_steroids.kill_tags:
      kill_known: true

The output is:

<p>Visible paragraph.</p>

<p>Visible  text.</p>

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Meaning kill list of str [] CSS selectors, or XPath expressions prefixed with !. Matching elements are removed with their content. kill_known bool false Also remove <del> elements and code blocks in the del language. kill_empty list of str ["p", "div", "h1", "h2", "h3", "h4", "h5", "h6", "pre"] Tag names. Elements with these names are removed when they have no text and no attributes. normalize bool false Pass the HTML through BeautifulSoup (html5lib) before and after the removal.

normalize adds a document wrapper

html5lib builds a full document, so with normalize: true the output is wrapped in <html><head></head><body>…</body></html>. Leave it off when the output is inserted into a page, as in MkDocs.

Empty elements with attributes are kept

An empty element that has any attribute, such as <div class="spacer"></div> or <p id="x"></p>, is not removed by kill_empty. An element that only contains an image with a src is kept for the same reason.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - pymdownx.tilde
  - mdx_steroids.kill_tags:
      kill:
        - .advertisement-banner
        - "!//figure[not(img)]"
      kill_known: true
      kill_empty: [p, div, span]

Python, with an XPath selector:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    '<div id="x">X</div>\n\nKeep.',
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.kill_tags"],
    extension_configs={"mdx_steroids.kill_tags": {"kill": ["!//div[@id='x']"]}},
)
# <p>Keep.</p>

docs.title: md_mako
docs.text: mdx_steroids.md_mako runs the Markdown source through the Mako template engine before Python-Markdown parses it. You can use variables, Python expressions, loops, conditions and included files in your Markdown.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Configuration:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.meta_yaml
  - mdx_steroids.md_mako:
      meta:
        product: FontLab
        author: Nobody

Markdown:

---
author: John Doe
---
## Heading

${author} wrote this for ${product}.

% for n in ['one', 'two']:
* ${n}
% endfor

HTML:

<h2>Heading</h2>
<p>John Doe wrote this for FontLab.</p>
<ul>
<li>one</li>
<li>two</li>
</ul>
  • meta_yaml removed the front matter and stored author: John Doe.
  • md_mako rendered the page with the variables from meta (product, author), then replaced author with the value from the front matter.
  • The % for loop produced one list item per value.
  • The ## Heading line stayed a heading, although ## starts a comment in Mako.

docs.title: Mako syntax in Markdown
docs.text:
Syntax Meaning ${expression} Insert the value of a Python expression % for …: … % endfor Loop; the % must be the first character on the line % if …: … % else: … % endif Condition <%include file="name.md"/> Insert another file, also rendered by Mako <%! … %> Module-level Python code, for example imports and functions <% … %> Python code that runs while the page is rendered %% at the start of a line A literal % ${"$"}{…} A literal ${…}

A % or $ in the middle of a line, as in 50% of users or $5, is kept as it is.

See the Mako documentation for the full syntax.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. If python_block names a file that exists, its content is put at the start of the source inside <%! … %>, so its functions and imports are available in the page.
  2. If include_auto is set, <%include file="…"/> for that file is put at the very start.
  3. Lines that start with #, {% or %} are protected so that Mako leaves them alone. This keeps Markdown headings, which Mako would read as comments (##), and template tags meant for other tools.
  4. The variables are collected: first everything from meta, then everything from md.Meta, if another extension such as meta_yaml has filled it. Front-matter keys are lower-cased, and list values are joined into one string. Front matter wins over meta.
  5. Mako renders the source with strict_undefined=True. The result replaces the source, and Python-Markdown continues with it.

The same heading protection applies to files loaded with <%include>.

docs.title: Order with meta_yaml
docs.text: meta_yaml runs before md_mako (priority 29 against 28), so the front matter is already parsed and removed when Mako runs. Without meta_yaml, the front matter is ordinary text: Mako passes it through, and Python-Markdown renders the --- lines as rules and the key: value line as text.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning meta dict {} Variables available in every page. Front matter overrides them. include_base str or list "." Folder, or list of folders, where <%include file="…"/> looks for files. Relative folders are resolved against the current working directory. include_encoding str "utf-8" Encoding of the page source passed to Mako. include_auto str "" A file included at the start of every page. An absolute path is split into folder and file name, and the folder is searched first. python_block str "" A Python file whose content is added at the start of every page as a <%! … %> block.

docs.title: python_block lookup
docs.text:
The extension looks for the python_block file in two places:

  1. The path as given, relative to the current working directory.
  2. include_base[0] joined with the path.

The second rule only works when include_base is a list. If include_base is a string, include_base[0] is its first character, so a string such as "includes" makes the extension look in a folder named i. Give include_base as a list, or give python_block as a path from the working directory:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.md_mako:
      include_base: [includes]
      python_block: helpers.py      # found as includes/helpers.py

If the file is not found in either place, the option is ignored without a message.

docs.title: Example with includes and helpers
docs.text:
Folder layout:

includes/
├── head.md        # *Draft for ${product}.*
├── notice.md      # Note: this page is about ${product}.
└── helpers.py

includes/helpers.py:

import datetime

def year():
    return datetime.date(2026, 1, 1).year

Configuration:

extension_configs = {
    "mdx_steroids.md_mako": {
        "include_base": ["includes"],
        "include_auto": "head.md",
        "python_block": "helpers.py",
        "meta": {"product": "FontLab"},
    }
}

Markdown, converted with meta_yaml and md_mako:

---
author: John Doe
---
## Heading

${author}, ${year()}.

<%include file="notice.md"/>

HTML:

<p><em>Draft for FontLab.</em></p>
<h2>Heading</h2>
<p>John Doe, 2026.</p>
<p>Note: this page is about FontLab.</p>

docs.title: Use front matter as variables
docs.text:
Load meta_yaml before md_mako. Every front-matter key becomes a variable with a lower-case name:

---
Title: Release notes
Version: 8.4
---
# ${title} for version ${version}

meta_yaml reads every value as a string, so ${version} prints 8.4.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
The extension does not catch Mako errors. They stop the conversion:

  • An undefined variable raises NameError, for example NameError: 'missing' is not defined, because strict_undefined is on.
  • A Mako syntax error, such as a % for without % endfor, raises a Mako exception.

In MkDocs, either error stops the build.

docs.title: meta_yaml
docs.text:
mdx_steroids.meta_yaml reads a YAML block at the top of a Markdown document, removes it from the text and stores the values in the Meta attribute of the Markdown object. It is by Bernhard Fisseni and based on the meta-data extension of Python-Markdown.

The extension has no options.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
import markdown

md = markdown.Markdown(extensions=["mdx_steroids.meta_yaml"])
html = md.convert("---\nTitle: Test Doc\nTags: [a, b]\nCount: 3\n---\n\nThe body.")
print(html)
print(md.Meta)

Output:

<p>The body.</p>
{'title': ['Test Doc'], 'tags': ['a', 'b'], 'count': ['3']}
  • The YAML block is not in the HTML.
  • Keys are lower-cased: Title became title.
  • Every value is a list. A single value is wrapped in a list; a YAML list stays a list.
  • Every scalar is a string. 3 became '3'.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
The block must start on the first line of the document:

---
title: My page
author: Alex Doe
tags: [python, markdown]
---

The content starts here.
  • The first line is exactly ---.
  • The second line must look like a key: a word (letters, digits, _, -), optional spaces and a colon. Otherwise the --- is treated as a horizontal rule and nothing is read. This lets a document start with a rule.
  • The block ends at the first line that is exactly --- or ....

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension is a preprocessor with priority 29, so it runs before most other preprocessors, including md_mako (28).

  1. It sets md.Meta to an empty dict.
  2. If the first line is --- and the second line looks like key:, it collects lines up to the closing --- or ... and removes them from the document.
  3. It parses the collected lines with PyYAML's BaseLoader (the C version, CBaseLoader, when available). BaseLoader does not convert types, so numbers, booleans and dates stay strings.
  4. It lower-cases the top-level keys, wraps each value that is not a list in a list, and stores the result in md.Meta.

Nested mappings are kept as dicts inside the list:

---
title: A
nested:
  key: value
flag: true
---

gives {'title': ['A'], 'nested': [{'key': 'value'}], 'flag': ['true']}.

The value format, lower-case keys and lists, matches Python-Markdown's own meta extension, so tools written for that extension can read md.Meta.

docs.title: Reusing a Markdown object
docs.text:
md.Meta is reset at the start of each conversion. After md.convert("Two") on a document without front matter, md.Meta is {}.

For an empty document, Python-Markdown returns early without running the preprocessors. If the object has never converted a non-empty document, md.Meta does not exist yet.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
The extension does not catch YAML errors:

  • A block without a closing --- or ... takes the rest of the document as YAML, which usually fails with yaml.scanner.ScannerError.
  • Invalid YAML, such as title: [unclosed, raises a yaml exception such as ParserError.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
MkDocs reads front matter itself, before Markdown conversion, so you do not need this extension for MkDocs page metadata. Use it when you call Python-Markdown directly, or together with md_mako:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.meta_yaml
  - mdx_steroids.md_mako

docs.title: replimgsrc
docs.text: mdx_steroids.replimgsrc does a find-and-replace on the src of every image. Use it to point images that were written for one location, such as a GitHub repository, to another.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With find: https://github.com/repo/blob/master/images/ and replace: ../img/, this Markdown:

![Logo](https://github.com/repo/blob/master/images/logo.png)

becomes:

<p><img alt="Logo" src="../img/logo.png" /></p>

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
After Python-Markdown has built the document tree, the extension visits every <img> element:

  • If find is not empty, it replaces every occurrence of find in src with replace.
  • If find is empty, it puts replace in front of src.

With find empty and replace: /static/, ![Logo](logo.png) becomes <img alt="Logo" src="/static/logo.png" />. With both options empty, nothing changes.

The replacement is plain text, not a pattern, and it applies to absolute and relative paths alike. Images written as raw HTML are not in the document tree and are not changed.

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning find str "" The text to look for in each image src. replace str "" The replacement text, or a prefix when find is empty.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.replimgsrc:
      find: https://github.com/repo/blob/master/images/
      replace: ../img/

Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    "![Logo](logo.png)",
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.replimgsrc"],
    extension_configs={"mdx_steroids.replimgsrc": {"replace": "/static/"}},
)
# <p><img alt="Logo" src="/static/logo.png" /></p>

docs.title: replimgsrc or absimgsrc
docs.text:
replimgsrc absimgsrc Changes Every image Only relative images Method Text replacement, or a prefix URL join with urljoin() Typical use Move images from one known location to another Serve all local images from a CDN

Both run as tree processors with priority 0, so the one you load first runs first. With absimgsrc (base_url: https://cdn/) loaded before replimgsrc (replace: /s/), ![a](x.png) becomes src="/s/https://cdn/x.png". In the opposite order it becomes src="https://cdn/s/x.png".

docs.title: translate_no
docs.text: mdx_steroids.translate_no adds translate="no" and the class notranslate to chosen HTML elements. Browser translation tools, such as the one built into Chrome, leave elements marked this way untranslated. By default it marks code, key names and highlighted text.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the default options, and with keys and pymdownx.mark also loaded, this Markdown:

Use `print()` and ++ctrl+c++ ==here==.

becomes:

<p>Use <code translate="no" class="notranslate">print()</code> and <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-control notranslate" translate="no">Ctrl</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-c notranslate" translate="no">C</kbd></span> <mark translate="no" class="notranslate">here</mark>.</p>

The <code>, <kbd> and <mark> elements are marked. Existing classes, such as key-control, are kept.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension is a postprocessor: it runs on the finished HTML string.

  1. If normalize is true, it reparses the HTML with BeautifulSoup and html5lib.
  2. It parses the HTML with lxml.html.fromstring().
  3. It converts each entry of add to XPath. An entry that starts with ! is used as XPath directly; any other entry is a CSS selector and is converted with cssselect.
  4. For every element that matches, it sets translate="no" and adds the class notranslate.
  5. It serialises the tree back to HTML. If normalize is true, it runs BeautifulSoup over the result again.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Type Default Meaning add list of str ["code", "mark", "pre", "kbd"] CSS selectors, or XPath expressions prefixed with !, of the elements to mark. normalize bool false Pass the HTML through BeautifulSoup (html5lib) before and after marking. With this option the output is wrapped in <html><head></head><body>…</body></html>.

Setting add replaces the default list. To keep the defaults and add more, list them all:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.translate_no:
      add: [code, mark, pre, kbd, .product-name]

With add: [strong], Use the **Glyph** panel. becomes:

<p>Use the <strong translate="no" class="notranslate">Glyph</strong> panel.</p>

docs.title: Output with several top-level elements
docs.text: lxml.html.fromstring() wraps a fragment with several top-level elements in a <div>. A document of two paragraphs therefore comes back as <div><p>…</p><p>…</p></div>. Take this into account if your CSS or later processing expects the paragraphs at the top level.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    "Use `print()`.",
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.translate_no"],
)
# <p>Use <code translate="no" class="notranslate">print()</code>.</p>

MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.keys
  - mdx_steroids.translate_no

docs.title: wikilink
docs.text: mdx_steroids.wikilink turns wiki-style links, [[Page Name]], into Markdown links. The page name becomes the link text, and a URL is built from the page name.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
With the default options, this Markdown:

This is a [[Wiki Link]] and [[Ünïcode Page]].

becomes:

<p>This is a <a href="/Wiki-Link/">Wiki Link</a> and <a href="/%C3%9Cn%C3%AFcode-Page/">Ünïcode Page</a>.</p>

With base_url: /kb/, end_url: .html and space_sep: _:

This is a [[Wiki Link]].

<p>This is a <a href="/kb/Wiki_Link.html">Wiki Link</a>.</p>

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The extension is a preprocessor: it rewrites the Markdown source before Python-Markdown parses it.

  1. On every line it finds [[…]] where the text inside contains no brackets and no line break.
  2. It builds a slug from the text with the slugify function of pymdownx.slugs, with case kept as it is (case="none") and percent encoding on. Spaces become space_sep; punctuation such as &, : and ! is dropped; letters outside ASCII are percent-encoded.
  3. It replaces [[Text]] with the Markdown link [Text](base_url + slug + end_url).

Python-Markdown then turns that link into an <a> element.

Some results of step 2, with the default options:

Markdown href [[a]] /a/ [[b c]] /b-c/ [[C++ & Python: tips!]] /C--Python-tips/ [[Ünïcode Page]] /%C3%9Cn%C3%AFcode-Page/

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Option Type Default Meaning base_url str "/" Text put before the slug. end_url str "/" Text put after the slug. space_sep str "-" Text that replaces spaces in the slug. html_class str "wikilink" Accepted but not used. The links have no class, because Python-Markdown builds them from ordinary Markdown links.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• No custom link text. [[Page Name|Label]] is not split at |. It becomes a link with the text Page Name|Label to /Page-NameLabel/. Write an ordinary Markdown link instead: [Label](/Page-Name/).
  • Case is kept. [[Getting Started]] links to /Getting-Started/. MkDocs builds URLs from file names, which are often lower case, such as getting-started/. Name the target file to match, or use ordinary links.
  • Code is not protected. The extension works on raw lines, so `[[code]]` in inline code becomes `[code](/code/)`.
  • In MkDocs, links that start with / are reported as absolute links and are not checked.

docs.title: Configuration examples
docs.text:
MkDocs:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.wikilink:
      base_url: /wiki/
      end_url: /
      space_sep: "-"

Python:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    "See [[Wiki Link]].",
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.wikilink"],
    extension_configs={"mdx_steroids.wikilink": {"base_url": "/kb/", "end_url": ".html"}},
)
# <p>See <a href="/kb/Wiki-Link.html">Wiki Link</a>.</p>

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Every extension takes its options as keyword arguments. Python-Markdown passes them in from extension_configs, from a -c file on the command line, or from the markdown_extensions list in MkDocs. This page shows the three forms and summarises the options of all extensions.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Use the dotted extension name as the key in extension_configs:

import markdown

html = markdown.markdown(
    text,
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.absimgsrc", "mdx_steroids.kill_tags"],
    extension_configs={
        "mdx_steroids.absimgsrc": {"base_url": "https://cdn.example.com/"},
        "mdx_steroids.kill_tags": {"kill": [".draft"], "kill_known": True},
    },
)

You can also create the extension object yourself. Every module has a makeExtension() function that accepts the options:

from mdx_steroids.absimgsrc import makeExtension

html = markdown.markdown(text, extensions=[makeExtension(base_url="https://cdn.example.com/")])

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
python -m markdown -c FILE reads a JSON or YAML file with the same structure as extension_configs. Load each configured extension with -x as well:

python -m markdown -x mdx_steroids.absimgsrc -c config.yml input.md

docs.title: MkDocs
docs.text:
Give the options under the extension name in markdown_extensions:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.absimgsrc:
      base_url: https://cdn.example.com/
  - mdx_steroids.kill_tags:
      kill:
        - .draft
      kill_known: true

An extension without options is listed by name alone:

markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.comments

docs.title: All options
docs.text:
Extension Option Type Default absimgsrc base_url str "" comments — figcap — img_smart find str "" repl_path str "" repl_url str "" alt_figure bool false cache str "" lazy bool false interlink base_url str "" end_url str "" keys, kbd separator str "+" strict bool false class str "keys" camel_case bool false key_map dict {} kill_tags normalize bool false kill list of str [] kill_known bool false kill_empty list of str ["p", "div", "h1", "h2", "h3", "h4", "h5", "h6", "pre"] md_mako include_base str or list "." include_encoding str "utf-8" include_auto str "" python_block str "" meta dict {} meta_yaml — replimgsrc find str "" replace str "" translate_no normalize bool false add list of str ["code", "mark", "pre", "kbd"] wikilink base_url str "/" end_url str "/" space_sep str "-" html_class str "wikilink" (not used)

Each extension page explains its options in detail.

docs.title: Combining extensions
docs.text:
Some extensions are designed to work together:

  • meta_yaml with md_mako: the YAML front matter becomes template variables. See md_mako.
  • keys with translate_no: translate_no marks the <kbd> elements that keys creates, so browser translation leaves key names alone.
  • kill_tags with pymdownx.tilde: ~~text~~ becomes <del>, which kill_known: true removes.

Do not combine absimgsrc, replimgsrc and img_smart without checking the result: all three change image src attributes. See Architecture for the order in which they run.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or later.

Installing the package also installs everything the extensions import:

Package Minimum version Used by markdown 3.5 All extensions pymdown-extensions 10.2 keys (escape handling), wikilink (slugs) mako 1.3 md_mako PyYAML 6.0 meta_yaml lxml 5.0 kill_tags, translate_no cssselect 1.2 kill_tags, translate_no (CSS selectors) beautifulsoup4 4.12 kill_tags, translate_no (normalize option) html5lib 1.1 kill_tags, translate_no (normalize option) filetype 1.2 img_smart imageio 2.0 img_smart requests 2.0 img_smart (remote images) json-flatten 0.3 Listed as a dependency; not imported by any extension

docs.title: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
pip install vexy-python-markdown-steroids

With uv:

uv pip install vexy-python-markdown-steroids

For an MkDocs site, install the package into the same environment as MkDocs. To try it in a one-off build without installing:

uvx --with vexy-python-markdown-steroids mkdocs build

docs.title: Install from source
docs.text:
1. Clone the repository:

    git clone https://github.com/vexyart/vexy-python-markdown-steroids.git
cd vexy-python-markdown-steroids

  2. Install it with the development tools:

    uv sync --extra dev

The version comes from the latest vX.Y.Z git tag through hatch-vcs.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
The import name is mdx_steroids, not the PyPI name:

python -c "import mdx_steroids; print(mdx_steroids.__version__)"

To check that an extension loads, convert a short string with it:

python -c "import markdown; print(markdown.markdown('Press ++ctrl+s++.', extensions=['mdx_steroids.keys']))"

The command prints:

<p>Press <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-control">Ctrl</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-s">S</kbd></span>.</p>

Video sizes in img_smart

img_smart reads video dimensions with the pyav plugin of imageio. That plugin needs the av package, which is not installed automatically. Without it, videos get no width. Install it with pip install av if you need video sizes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
This page uses two extensions, wikilink and keys, in three ways: from Python, from the python -m markdown command and from MkDocs. The input is the same each time:

# Notes

See [[Getting Started]] and press ++ctrl+s++ to save.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • The package is installed (see Installation).

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
1. Pass the extension names to markdown.markdown():

    import markdown

text = "# Notes\n\nSee [[Getting Started]] and press ++ctrl+s++ to save."
html = markdown.markdown(
    text,
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.wikilink", "mdx_steroids.keys"],
)
print(html)

  2. Run the script. It prints:

    <h1>Notes</h1>
<p>See <a href="/Getting-Started/">Getting Started</a> and press <span class="keys"><kbd class="key-control">Ctrl</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-s">S</kbd></span> to save.</p>

What happened:

  • wikilink replaced [[Getting Started]] with the Markdown link [Getting Started](/Getting-Started/) before parsing. The default base_url and end_url are both /, and spaces become -.
  • keys turned ++ctrl+s++ into a <span class="keys"> with one <kbd> per key and a <span>+</span> between them.

To change options, pass extension_configs:

html = markdown.markdown(
    text,
    extensions=["mdx_steroids.wikilink", "mdx_steroids.keys"],
    extension_configs={
        "mdx_steroids.wikilink": {"base_url": "/wiki/", "end_url": ".html"},
        "mdx_steroids.keys": {"strict": True},
    },
)

The link now points to /wiki/Getting-Started.html, and the keys are wrapped in an outer <kbd class="keys"> instead of a <span>.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Python-Markdown has a command-line interface. It reads extension options from a JSON or YAML file.

  1. Save the Markdown as input.md.

  2. Save the options as config.yml:

    mdx_steroids.wikilink:
  base_url: /wiki/
  end_url: .html
mdx_steroids.keys:
  strict: true

  3. Run:

    python -m markdown -x mdx_steroids.wikilink -x mdx_steroids.keys -c config.yml input.md -f output.html

output.html contains:

<h1>Notes</h1>
<p>See <a href="/wiki/Getting-Started.html">Getting Started</a> and press <kbd class="keys"><kbd class="key-control">Ctrl</kbd><span>+</span><kbd class="key-s">S</kbd></kbd> to save.</p>

Every extension named in config.yml must also be loaded with -x.

docs.title: From MkDocs
docs.text:
1. Install the package into the environment that runs MkDocs.

  2. Add the extensions to markdown_extensions in mkdocs.yml:

    markdown_extensions:
  - mdx_steroids.wikilink:
      base_url: /
      end_url: /
  - mdx_steroids.keys

  3. Run mkdocs build.

MkDocs passes each page through the extensions. In the built page, the text reads "See Getting Started and press Ctrl+S to save", with a link and styled keys.

Note

MkDocs reports a link that starts with / as an absolute link and leaves it unchanged. wikilink keeps the capital letters of the page name, so [[Getting Started]] links to /Getting-Started/. Make sure the target page has that URL; see wikilink.
